name: Ittai the Gittite
charge: As the Lord liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be
summary: As David fled from Absalom, all his servants passed on beside him, and with them the Gittites, six hundred men that came after him from Gath. David told Ittai to go back, because he was a stranger and an exile who had come only yesterday, and the king would not make him go up and down with him when he himself did not know where he was going. Ittai swore by the Lord and by the king’s life to be with him in death or in life, and passed over with all his men and all the little ones. When the army was set in array, a third part of it was under his hand.
offenseFull: All his servants passed on beside him, and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king. The king asked Ittai the Gittite why he went with them too, and told him to return to his place and abide with the king, for he was a stranger and also an exile; he came but yesterday, and should the king this day make him go up and down with them, seeing the king himself was going wherever he could? He told him to return and take back his brethren, and mercy and truth be with him (2 Samuel 15:18-19; 2 Samuel 15:18-20). The king gave him leave to go and made him no promise of what would come of staying. Ittai answered with an oath by the Lord and by the life of the king, that in what place the king should be, whether in death or life, even there also would his servant be. David said, go and pass over, and Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones that were with him (2 Samuel 15:20-22; 2 Samuel 15:21-22). Ittai showed a level of loyalty that David respected, and so David let him come; that loyalty in the face of trouble is the thing seen all through Israel’s story. His oath named death as well as life, so it was not a bargain made on a guaranteed reward. All the country wept with a loud voice as the people passed over the brook Kidron toward the wilderness (2 Samuel 15:18-23; 2 Samuel 15:23), and the contrast is sharp: the king’s own son, who came forth of his bowels, was seeking his life, while a stranger the king had offered to release bound himself to the king’s danger.
judgmentFull: David numbered the people that were with him and set captains of thousands and captains of hundreds over them, and sent forth a third part under the hand of Joab, a third under the hand of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third under the hand of Ittai the Gittite (2 Samuel 18:1-2; 2 Samuel 18:2). The man who had pledged to stay with the king in death or in life was trusted with a third of the army. When David said he would surely go forth with them himself, the people answered that he should not go, for he was worth ten thousand of them, and it was better that he succour them out of the city; and the king hearkened to their counsel and said he would do what seemed best to them (2 Samuel 18:2-4). He did not run a dictatorship, and in a time when he could not trust his own flesh and blood he trusted the proven men he had warred with for years. Then the king commanded Joab and Abishai and Ittai to deal gently for his sake with the young man Absalom, and all the people heard when the king gave all the captains charge concerning him (2 Samuel 18:1-5; 2 Samuel 18:5). Of the three captains it was Joab, and not the stranger out of Gath, who broke that charge. The road out of Jerusalem showed who would stand when the favour of the throne no longer promised anything, and Ittai gave his word on that road, before any honour was in sight.
